records.quote: Corollary 3.1. The s−IFRA monotonicity does not have the hereditary property.

records.quote: Corollary 4.1. Let X be s−IFR, for some s ≥ 1, random variable, with distribution function F ∈ F and density function f . Let Y(n) = max(Y1 , . . . , Yn ) where Yi are independent with tail function T̄ X,s (x). Then Y(n) is s−IFR, for every s ≥ 1.

records.compared: Parallel maximum Y(n) against the exponential reference (s-IFR class)

hypotheses.text: X s-IFR; Y1,...,Yn iid with survival function T̄_{X,s}

conclusion.direction: Y(n) is s-IFR for every s >= 1 (equivalently Y(n) <=s-IFR Exp by Theorem 2.1)

records.ambiguity: Closure/class-membership claim for the parallel system; equivalently an s-IFR ordering against the exponential.

note: In scope: class-heredity/closure claim equivalent to an s-IFR ordering vs the exponential via Theorem 2.1; pass A one-sided, verdict matches.

records.quote: Corollary 7.1. Let X and Y be defined as in (7.1). Then T̄_{Y,s}(T̄_{X,s}^{-1}(x))/x ≤ 1, for every x > 0.
records.family: X = max of two iid Exp(mean 1); Y = max{Y1,Y2}, Y1 ~ Exp(1), Y2 ~ Exp(1/lambda), lambda > 1, as in (7.1)
records.compared: Ordering function c_s(x) = T̄_{Y,s}(T̄_{X,s}^{-1}(x)) bounded by the diagonal

hypotheses.text: X, Y as in (7.1); uses Proposition 7.1's T̄_{X,s}(x) >= T̄_{Y,s}(x) for all x >= 0

conclusion.direction: T̄_{Y,s}(T̄_{X,s}^{-1}(x))/x <= 1 for all x > 0 (the s-IFRA ordering function t_s(x) <= 1)

records.ambiguity: Pass A's quote had the inverse attached to T̄_{Y,s}; per the paper (and consistency with Definition 2.4/Proposition 7.2) the statement is T̄_{Y,s}(T̄_{X,s}^{-1}(x))/x <= 1. This is the c_s ordering-function bound underlying the s-IFRA ordering of Proposition 7.2.

note: Quote corrected: the inverse applies to T̄_{X,s}, not T̄_{Y,s} (pass A mis-transcribed). Order coded 'ageing: s-IFRA' since it bounds the star-ordering function c_s(x)/x.

records.quote: Example 3.1. Let X be a nonnegative random variable with density function f (x) = (x2 + c)e−x /(c + 2). ... By choosing c ∈ (0, 2) we obtain rX,1 that starts decreasing and eventually becomes increasing, while rX,2 is increasing. That is, X is not 1−IFR but is 2−IFR. Moreover, it is also easy to verify that X is not 1−IFRA.
records.compared: 1-IFR / 1-IFRA vs 2-IFR class membership of a single distribution

hypotheses.text: f(x) = (x^2 + c) e^{-x}/(c+2); choose c in (0,2); r_{X,1} eventually increasing after decreasing start; r_{X,2} increasing

conclusion.direction: X is 2-IFR but is not 1-IFR and not 1-IFRA — hence (s+1)-IFR does not imply s-IFR and s-IFRA is not hereditary (with Proposition 3.1, yields Corollary 3.1)

records.ambiguity: Class-membership example used to witness non-heredity of s-IFRA.

note: Both passes kept it; it is a counterexample-style class-membership claim (not a pairwise ordering) witnessing Corollary 3.1's non-heredity; canonical order 'ageing: s-IFR' family.

records.quote: Lemma 3.1. Let X be a nonnegative random variable. For every integer s ≥ 1, the following relations hold. a) If X is s−IFR, then X is (s + 1)−IFR. b) If X is s−DFR, then X is (s + 1)−DFR.
records.compared: s-IFR/s-DFR class nesting across iteration levels

hypotheses.text: X s-IFR (part a) or s-DFR (part b)

conclusion.direction: s-IFR implies (s+1)-IFR and s-DFR implies (s+1)-DFR (classes nested upward)

records.ambiguity: Class-membership (heredity) result, not a pairwise ordering; via Theorem 2.1 equivalently X <=s-IFR Exp implies X <=(s+1)-IFR Exp. Attributed to Theorem 2 in Navarro and Hernández [28].

note: In scope by the audit's broad reading of ageing-order claims (class nesting = ordering vs exponential comparator via Theorem 2.1); pass A one-sided.

Proposition 4.1 gives moment inequalities for E(X-x)_+^k under s-IFR/s-DFR — it characterizes a single distribution's moments, not an ordering of two distributions; out of scope per spec ('results that only characterize one distribution (moments, shape, estimation)').

records.claim: Remark 7.2 (counterexample to iterated Kochar-Xu conjecture, s = 2)
records.quote: Remark 7.2. ... Write, for simplicity, X = max{X1 , X2 } and Y = max{Y1 , Y2 } and consider Vs (x) = T̄ Y,s (x) − T̄ X,s (ax), where a > 0. ... If we choose the parameters (s, λ1 /λ2 , θ1 /θ2 , a) = (2, 0.34, 11, 2.89) the sign variation of Vs (x) is “−, +, −” so, according to Theorem 2.2, X and Y are not comparable with respect to the 2−IFRA order, hence they cannot be comparable with respect to the 2−IFR order. ... (λ1 , λ2 , θ1 , θ2 ) = (1/1474)(408, 1200, 134, 1474)ϑ, with ϑ > 0, generates a whole family of counter-examples for the conjecture when the iteration parameter s = 2.
records.family: Two-component parallel systems of independent exponentials; rate vectors (lambda1,lambda2) majorized by (theta1,theta2) with lambda1+lambda2 = theta1+theta2
records.compared: X = max{X1,X2} vs Y = max{Y1,Y2} under majorized rate vectors

hypotheses.text: Kochar-Xu setup: majorized rate vectors would conjecturally give X <=s-IFR Y; here s=2, lambda1/lambda2=0.34, theta1/theta2=11, a=2.89

conclusion.direction: X and Y are not comparable in the 2-IFRA order (sign variation of V_s is -,+,-), hence not in the 2-IFR order; the iterated Kochar-Xu conjecture fails at s = 2

records.quantifiers: s = 2; n = 2; theta > 0 scaling gives a family of counterexamples
records.ambiguity: The s = 1 case of the Kochar-Xu conjecture remains unresolved.

note: Both passes agreed on substance; canonical order 'ageing: 2-IFRA' (relative/iterated ageing order), and the no-comparability verdict is verbatim.

records.quote: Theorem 2.1. Let X be a random variable with distribution function FX ∈ F and Y be an exponential random variable. Then, 1. X is s−IFR if and only if X ≤s−IFR Y . Similarly, X is s−DFR if and only if Y ≤s−IFR X .
records.family: F non-negative lifetimes vs exponential Y
records.compared: X vs exponential Y

hypotheses.text: Y exponential

conclusion.direction: X s-IFR iff X <=s-IFR Y; X s-DFR iff Y <=s-IFR X (equivalences against the exponential reference)

records.ambiguity: Stated from Nanda et al. [27] (Theorem 3.2). Establishes the exponential as the boundary element of the s-IFR class.

records.quote: Theorem 2.1. ... 2. X is s−IFRA if and only if X ≤s−IFRA Y . Similarly, X is s−DFRA if and only if Y ≤s−IFRA X .

records.quote: Theorem 2.2. Let X and Y be random variables with distribution functions FX , FY ∈ F , respectively. 1. We have X ≤s−IFR Y if, and only if, the sign variation of T̄ Y,s (x) − T̄ X,s (ax + b) is, at most, “+, −, +”, for every a ∈ R and b ∈ R (the case a > 0 and b ∈ R is sufficient, based on Remark 2.1).
records.compared: X vs Y under the sign-variation criterion on T̄_{Y,s}(x) - T̄_{X,s}(ax+b)

hypotheses.text: FX, FY in F; sign variation of T̄_{Y,s}(x) - T̄_{X,s}(ax+b) at most '+,-,+' for all a,b (a>0 suffices)

conclusion.direction: X <=s-IFR Y iff the sign-variation bound holds

records.quantifiers: s >= 1; all a > 0, b in R

records.quote: Theorem 2.2. ... 2. We have X ≤s−IFRA Y if, and only if, the sign variation of T̄ Y,s (x) − T̄ X,s (ax) is, at most, “−, +”, for every a ∈ R.
records.compared: X vs Y under the sign-variation criterion on T̄_{Y,s}(x) - T̄_{X,s}(ax)

hypotheses.text: FX, FY in F; sign variation of T̄_{Y,s}(x) - T̄_{X,s}(ax) at most '-,+' for all a>0

conclusion.direction: X <=s-IFRA Y iff the sign-variation bound holds

note: In scope: sign-change characterizations of the s-IFR and s-IFRA orders; split into one record per order.

records.quote: Theorem 2.3. Let X and Y be random variables with absolutely continuous distribution functions FX , FY ∈ F , such that limx→∞ (FY (x)/FX (x)) = l ∈ [0, ∞). Then FX ≤s−IFR FY if either of the following two conditions holds for the function Hs (x) = T̄ Y,s (x) − T̄ X,s (ax + b) (or the corresponding version Hs−1 for Ps (x) − Ps−1 (ax + b)): for every a > 0 and b ∈ R, the sign variation of Hs (x) is at most '+,-' (one crossing), or the sign variation is at most '-,+' with the stated crossing conditions on the derivative.
records.compared: X vs Y (sufficient sign-variation criterion for s-IFR)

hypotheses.text: lim FY/FX = l in [0,infty); for every a>0, b in R the sign variation of H_s (or the P_s/P_{s-1} analogue) meets the stated crossing conditions

conclusion.direction: FX <=s-IFR FY under the sign-variation criterion

records.quantifiers: s >= 1; all a > 0, b in R
records.ambiguity: Theorem 2.3 is quoted from Theorem 3.1 in [3]; the text-layer formula is compressed, so the quote paraphrases the printed sign-variation clauses verbatim intent. See PDF for exact clause wording.

note: In scope: sufficient criterion for the s-IFR ordering (ageing order); pass A one-sided.

records.quote: Theorem 2.4. Let X and Y be random variables with absolutely continuous distribution functions FX , FY ∈ F such that limx→∞ (FY (x)/FX (x)) = l ∈ [0, ∞). Then FX ≤s−IFRA FY whenever the sign variation of Hs (x) = T̄ Y,s (x) − T̄ X,s (ax) (equivalently Ps (x) − Ps−1 (ax)) is at most '−, +' for every a > 0.

conclusion.direction: FX <=s-IFRA FY under the sign-variation criterion

records.quote: Theorem 6.1. Let X and Y be random variables with distribution functions FX , FY ∈ F , respectively. Assume that, for each a > 0 and b ≥ 0, the function Hs (x) = T̄ Y,s (x) − T̄ X,s (ax + b) changes sign at most once, and when a change occurs it is from '−' to '+'. If X ≤s−IFRA Y , then X ≤s−IFR Y .

hypotheses.text: X <=s-IFRA Y; for each a>0, b>=0, H_s(x) = T̄_{Y,s}(x) - T̄_{X,s}(ax+b) has at most one sign change, from '-' to '+'

conclusion.direction: X <=s-IFR Y

note: In scope: upgrades s-IFRA ordering to s-IFR under a crossing condition; canonical label 'ageing: s-IFR'.
